Choose optimal action there.
Replace that subgame with its continuation payoff.
Move backward until the root.

Common pitfall: using non-credible threats (actions that wouldn’t be optimal if reached).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE)

Write types and prior \(\Pr(\theta)\).
Strategy is type-contingent: \(a_i=s_i(\theta_i)\).
For each type, compute expected payoff for each action.
Choose best responses for each type; verify consistency across players.

Common pitfall: forgetting strategies are functions of type, not single actions.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
A PBE is (strategies, beliefs) satisfying: - Sequential rationality: actions optimal at every information set. - Bayes consistency on-path: update beliefs using Bayes’ rule where possible.

Standard workflow (signaling/screening)

Guess form: separating / pooling / semi-separating.
Propose strategies for sender types + receiver actions.
Compute on-path posteriors via Bayes.
Check receiver best responses given beliefs.
Check each sender type’s incentive constraints (no profitable deviations).
Specify off-path beliefs (carefully) and re-check deviations.

Common pitfall: not stating off-path beliefs, or using off-path beliefs that “magically” punish deviations without justification (sequential equilibrium addresses this).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Sequential equilibrium (SE)
Sequential equilibrium is PBE + a discipline on beliefs: - Beliefs must be limits of Bayes-updated beliefs from fully mixed trembles.

Practical use
If your PBE relies heavily on off-path beliefs: 1) Add tiny tremble probabilities to every action. 2) Compute implied posteriors. 3) Take limits → see which beliefs are justifiable. 4) Re-check optimality.
Common pitfall: treating off-path beliefs as completely free.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)

Receiver ignores message: same action after every message.
Beliefs stay at the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring).
Sender is indifferent over messages because messages don’t affect actions.

Use: baseline; compare informative equilibria against it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Trembling-hand perfect equilibrium

Start from a Nash equilibrium.
Ask whether it survives when opponents sometimes make small mistakes.
Equilibria relying on “impossible” actions not happening can fail.

Heuristic: if an equilibrium uses weakly dominated actions or fragile indifference, perfection may eliminate it.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Proper equilibrium
Like perfect equilibrium, but: - very bad mistakes are much less likely than slightly bad mistakes.
Use: sharper selection when perfection is not selective enough.

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Correlated equilibrium (CE)

Specify a distribution over action profiles (recommendations).
For each player and each recommendation, write obedience constraints: following ≥ deviating.
If all constraints hold, it’s a CE.

Memory aid: “Follow the recommendation because conditional on it, deviating doesn’t help.”

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Recipe card: Rationalizability

Iteratively delete strictly dominated actions.
Repeat in the reduced game until no more deletions.
Remaining actions are rationalizable.

Common pitfall: weak dominance deletion can be order-dependent (start with strict).

title: Equilibrium cheat sheet
text:
Mini glossary (quick)

NE: best response to best response.
SPE: NE in every subgame (credible).
BNE: NE with types; best response in expectation.
PBE: strategies + beliefs; Bayes on-path; sequentially rational.
SE: PBE + tremble-consistent beliefs.
CE: equilibrium over distributions; “obey the signal.”
Rationalizability: what survives iterated strict dominance.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
In cheap talk, messages are costless and non-binding. A babbling equilibrium is one in which messages convey no information: the receiver’s action does not depend on the message, and the sender is indifferent across messages.
Babbling equilibria exist very generally and serve as a baseline.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
In cheap talk, messages are costless and non-binding. A babbling equilibrium is one in which messages convey no information: the receiver’s action does not depend on the message, and the sender is indifferent across messages.
Babbling equilibria exist very generally and serve as a baseline.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Where it shows up

Cheap talk models (sender–receiver)
Communication settings with strong preference misalignment
As the “uninformative” benchmark when discussing informative equilibria (partition, separating)

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Make the receiver ignore messages: choose the same action after any message.
Set receiver beliefs equal to the prior (or any belief consistent with ignoring messages).
Verify receiver optimality under those beliefs.
Verify sender indifference: since messages don’t affect actions, any message is optimal.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Solved example (fully worked)

Problem (context + question)
A sender observes \(\theta\in\{0,1\}\) with prior \(\Pr(\theta=1)=1/2\). Sender sends costless message \(m\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}\). Receiver chooses action \(a\in\{0,1\}\).
Receiver payoff: \[
u_R(a,\theta)=\mathbf{1}\{a=\theta\}.
\]
Sender payoff (biased toward \(a=1\)): \[
u_S(a,\theta)=\mathbf{1}\{a=1\}.
\]
Question: Exhibit a babbling equilibrium (strategies + beliefs) and verify it.


Solution
A babbling equilibrium has receiver ignore the message.
Step 1 (receiver best response when ignoring messages): Under the prior, \(\Pr(\theta=1)=1/2\). Then - payoff from \(a=1\) is \(1/2\), - payoff from \(a=0\) is \(1/2\).
Receiver is indifferent, so a valid best response is: \[
a=0 \quad \text{after both messages}.
\]
Step 2 (sender incentives): If the receiver always plays \(a=0\), sender payoff is always \(0\) regardless of message. So the sender is indifferent and can send any message.
Let sender strategy be: always send “high”.
Step 3 (beliefs): Receiver beliefs do not depend on the message (since messages are ignored). Keep the prior: \[
\Pr(\theta=1\mid m)=1/2 \quad \text{for both } m\in\{\text{low},\text{high}\}.
\]
Result (babbling equilibrium): - Sender: always send “high”. - Receiver: always choose \(a=0\). - Beliefs: posterior equals prior after any message.


Check

Receiver optimality: given prior, \(a=0\) is a best response (ties).
Sender optimality: given receiver ignores messages, any message is optimal.
Beliefs are consistent with the equilibrium (receiver does not condition on \(m\)).



Takeaway
Babbling equilibria always exist because cheap messages can be ignored.

title: Babbling equilibrium (cheap talk)
text:
Later-on analysis

Informative equilibria require structure: partial alignment, restrictions on message space, or repeated interaction.
Adding costs converts cheap talk into signaling, where credibility can be restored.
Many refinements aim to rule out “unreasonable” beliefs or equilibria, but babbling is a genuine equilibrium prediction in many environments.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
A Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a pair (strategies, beliefs) in a dynamic game with incomplete information such that:

Sequential rationality: at every information set, each player’s action is optimal given their beliefs and others’ strategies.
Belief consistency (Bayes on-path): beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule wherever possible along the equilibrium path.

Off-path (zero-probability) histories require beliefs to be specified; this can create multiple PBEs.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
A Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is a pair (strategies, beliefs) in a dynamic game with incomplete information such that:

Sequential rationality: at every information set, each player’s action is optimal given their beliefs and others’ strategies.
Belief consistency (Bayes on-path): beliefs are updated using Bayes’ rule wherever possible along the equilibrium path.

Off-path (zero-probability) histories require beliefs to be specified; this can create multiple PBEs.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
Where it shows up

Signaling games (education, quality signals)
Screening models with dynamic interaction
Any extensive-form game with imperfect information

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Guess an equilibrium form (separating / pooling / semi-separating).
Specify strategies for all players.
Derive beliefs using Bayes’ rule on-path.
Check sequential rationality at every information set:

receiver best-responds given beliefs,
sender type best-responds given receiver strategy.

Specify off-path beliefs and verify no profitable deviations.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
section: Solved example (pooling PBE in a signaling game)
text:
Solved example (pooling PBE in a signaling game)

Problem (context + question)
Types: worker \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) with \(\Pr(H)=p\).
Worker chooses education \(e\in\{0,1\}\). Employer observes \(e\) and offers wage \(w\in\{w_H,w_L\}\).
Productivity: - If type \(H\): output value is \(2\) - If type \(L\): output value is \(1\)
Employer is competitive and pays expected productivity given beliefs: - pay \(w_H=2\) if believes \(H\) for sure, - pay \(w_L=1\) if believes \(L\) for sure, - pay \(w=p\cdot 2+(1-p)\cdot 1 = 1+p\) if belief is \(\Pr(H)=p\).
Education costs: - \(c_H(1)=0.2\), \(c_L(1)=0.8\), and \(c_H(0)=c_L(0)=0\).
Question: Construct a pooling PBE where both types choose \(e=0\).


Solution
We propose a pooling strategy: - Worker: \(e(\theta)=0\) for both \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\). - Employer: after observing \(e=0\), pay \(w(0)=1+p\) (belief equals prior); after \(e=1\), specify an off-path belief.
Step 1 (beliefs on-path): Since both types choose \(e=0\), observing \(e=0\) yields posterior \(\Pr(H\mid e=0)=p\). So paying \(w(0)=1+p\) is consistent.
Step 2 (employer sequential rationality): Given belief \(p\) after \(e=0\), competitive wage is \(1+p\). Good.
Now choose an off-path belief after \(e=1\). Let employer believe \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\) (i.e., “only low types deviate”), so employer pays \(w(1)=1\).
Step 3 (worker incentive constraints): - Type \(H\) payoff if follow pooling (\(e=0\)): \(1+p\). If deviate to \(e=1\): wage \(1\) minus cost \(0.2\) → \(1-0.2=0.8\). So \(H\) does not deviate if \(1+p \ge 0.8\), which holds for all \(p\in[0,1]\).

Type \(L\) payoff if follow pooling: \(1+p\). If deviate to \(e=1\): wage \(1\) minus cost \(0.8\) → \(0.2\). So \(L\) never deviates.

Result (pooling PBE): - Worker: both types choose \(e=0\). - Employer beliefs: \(\Pr(H\mid e=0)=p\); off-path set \(\Pr(H\mid e=1)=0\). - Employer wages: \(w(0)=1+p\), \(w(1)=1\).


Check

Beliefs on-path follow Bayes’ rule.
Actions are optimal at each information set given beliefs. So it is a PBE.



Takeaway
PBE requires beliefs; off-path beliefs can support pooling by punishing deviations.

title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE)
text:
Later-on analysis

Pooling PBEs can be fragile: refinements (sequential equilibrium, intuitive criterion) restrict off-path beliefs.
Separating PBEs require incentive compatibility inequalities (high type willing to signal; low type not).
PBE is a practical workhorse; just be explicit about beliefs and on/off-path behavior.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game that induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
Intuition: strategies must be credible not only along the equilibrium path but also after any possible history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
A subgame perfect equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game that induces a Nash equilibrium in every subgame.
Intuition: strategies must be credible not only along the equilibrium path but also after any possible history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Where it shows up

Extensive-form games with perfect information (classic backward induction)
Dynamic games where credibility of threats/promises matters
Bargaining models (alternating offers) are solved using SPE

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
How to solve (recipe)

Identify subgames (in perfect-information games, every decision node typically starts a subgame).
Solve the last subgames first (optimize at terminal decision nodes).
Replace each solved subgame by its continuation payoff.
Continue backward until the start: this is backward induction.
The resulting strategy profile is an SPE (in finite perfect-information games).

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Solved example (backward induction)

Problem (context + question)
A landlord (player 1) offers a rent increase: \(L\) (low) or \(H\) (high). The tenant (player 2) observes and chooses accept \(A\) or move \(M\).
Payoffs: - \((L,A)=(2,2)\), \((L,M)=(0,1)\) - \((H,A)=(3,0)\), \((H,M)=(0,1)\)
Question: Find the SPE.


Solution
Step 1 (solve tenant’s decision in each subgame): - After \(L\): tenant compares payoff \(2\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → chooses \(A\). - After \(H\): tenant compares payoff \(0\) (accept) vs \(1\) (move) → chooses \(M\).
So tenant strategy is: after \(L\) play \(A\), after \(H\) play \(M\).
Step 2 (landlord anticipates tenant’s response): - If landlord chooses \(L\), outcome is \((2,2)\). - If landlord chooses \(H\), tenant moves, outcome is \((0,1)\).
Landlord prefers \(L\) because \(2>0\).
Result (SPE): - Landlord plays \(L\). - Tenant plays \(A\) after \(L\) and \(M\) after \(H\). - Outcome: \((L,A)\).


Check

Tenant’s actions are optimal in each subgame.
Given tenant’s strategy, landlord’s choice is optimal at the start. So the strategy profile is Nash in every subgame.



Takeaway
SPE rules out non-credible threats by requiring optimal behavior after every history.

title: Subgame perfect equilibrium (SPE)
text:
Later-on analysis

With imperfect information, “subgame” may not be well-defined → PBE / sequential equilibrium.
With multiple SPE, equilibrium selection becomes a separate question.
In repeated games, SPE sets are large; punishments must still be credible.

title: Repeated games
text: A repeated game plays the same stage game over time (finitely or infinitely many periods). Strategies can condition on history.

title: Repeated games
text: A repeated game plays the same stage game over time (finitely or infinitely many periods). Strategies can condition on history.

title: Repeated games
text:
What’s special

Past behavior can be rewarded/punished → enables cooperation even when the one-shot game would not.
Central ideas: incentives over time, credibility, and equilibrium path vs off-path threats.
Infinite-horizon models often use a discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\).

title: Repeated games
section: One example (grim trigger in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma)
text:
One example (grim trigger in repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma)
Stage game: cooperate \(C\) or defect \(D\). Typical payoffs: - \((C,C)\) gives \((R,R)\), - \((D,C)\) gives \((T,S)\), - \((C,D)\) gives \((S,T)\), - \((D,D)\) gives \((P,P)\), with \(T>R>P>S\).
Grim trigger strategy: start with \(C\), continue \(C\) unless someone defects; after any defection, play \(D\) forever.
Incentive condition (intuition): cooperate today if the present temptation \(T-R\) is outweighed by the discounted future loss from punishment. Cooperation can be sustained if \(\delta\) is sufficiently high.

title: Repeated games
text:
Story
Two graduate students, Kai and Mira, share an office. Each week they decide whether to clean the shared space. Cleaning is effortful; skipping is tempting. If one keeps cleaning while the other skips, resentment builds. If both skip, the office becomes miserable.
Because the choice repeats, today’s action can trigger tomorrow’s response.

title: Repeated games
text:
Model

Stage actions: \(C\) (clean), \(S\) (shirk)
Stage payoffs (toy): PD-like
Infinite horizon with discount factor \(\delta\in(0,1)\)
Strategies can condition on history

title: Repeated games
text:
Equilibrium (cooperation via grim trigger)
Grim trigger: play \(C\) unless someone shirks; after any shirking, play \(S\) forever.
Compare deviating once vs cooperating on-path (player 1, symmetric): - Cooperate forever payoff: \(\frac{2}{1-\delta}\) - Deviate once (get 3 now, then punished with 1 forever): \(3 + \frac{\delta}{1-\delta}\)
Cooperation is sustainable if: \[
\frac{2}{1-\delta} \ge 3+\frac{\delta}{1-\delta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\delta \ge \frac12.
\]

title: Repeated games
text:
Later-on analysis

Finite horizon: backward induction kills cooperation near the end (unless there are other frictions).
Noisy actions: if mistakes happen, harsh punishments can be inefficient; “forgiving” strategies (tit-for-tat variants) become relevant.
Multiple equilibria: repeated games often admit many equilibrium paths; selection becomes a real question.

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text: Auctions allocate an item based on bids. Models differ by: - format (first-price, second-price, English, Dutch), - values (private values vs common values), - information (signals, asymmetries).

title: Auctions
text:
What’s special

Bidding strategies trade off winning probability vs payment.
In private values with risk-neutral bidders, many formats have linked outcomes (revenue equivalence under conditions).
In common-value settings, bidders fear the winner’s curse.

title: Auctions
text:
One example (second-price auction, private values)
Each bidder has value \(v_i\) for the item. In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid.
A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i = v_i.
\]
Intuition: your bid only affects whether you win, not what you pay conditional on winning. Overbidding risks winning at a price above your value; underbidding risks losing when you would have profited.

title: Auctions
text:
Story
A tutor releases one Saturday slot. Many students bid; each has private urgency. The rule for who pays what shapes bidding incentives.

title: Auctions
text:
Model

Bidders \(i=1,\dots,n\)
Private values \(v_i\)
Bids \(b_i\)
Auction format determines allocation and payment

title: Auctions
text:
Equilibrium (second-price auction)
In a second-price auction, the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. A dominant strategy is: \[
b_i=v_i.
\]
Reason (one-line): your bid affects winning, but the price conditional on winning is the opponent’s bid, not yours.

title: Auctions
text:
Later-on analysis

First-price auctions: equilibrium involves bid shading; risk aversion matters.
Common values: winner’s curse and information aggregation dominate.
Reserve prices and optimal design: mechanism design connects auctions to revenue maximization.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
A normal-form game models simultaneous choice: players pick actions without observing others’ choices.
A finite two-player game is often represented by payoff matrices \((A,B)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
A normal-form game models simultaneous choice: players pick actions without observing others’ choices.
A finite two-player game is often represented by payoff matrices \((A,B)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
What’s special

Strategies are complete plans chosen at once (pure or mixed).
Main solution concept: Nash equilibrium (possibly mixed).
Workhorse tools: best responses, dominance, indifference.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
One example (Prisoner’s Dilemma)
Actions: \(C\) (cooperate) or \(D\) (defect).
Payoffs: - \((C,C)=(2,2)\) - \((D,C)=(3,0)\) - \((C,D)=(0,3)\) - \((D,D)=(1,1)\)
Solution sketch. \(D\) strictly dominates \(C\) for each player, so the unique Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\), even though \((C,C)\) is Pareto-better.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Story
Two independent cafés, North Bean and South Bean, sit across the same narrow street by a commuter station. Tomorrow morning there will be a marathon: heavy demand, impatient customers, and intense competition for foot traffic. Tonight, each café must decide whether to run a deep discount.
If only one café discounts, it steals attention and most walk-ins. If both discount, they split the crowd but both suffer thin margins. If neither discounts, both do fine—yet each fears being the only one who doesn’t discount.
They decide simultaneously: no café observes the other’s choice before committing.

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Model

Players: cafés \(1,2\)
Actions: \(D\) (discount), \(N\) (normal)
Timing: simultaneous
Payoffs: profits

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Payoffs (toy)
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& D & N\\ \hline
D & (1,1) & (3,0)\\
N & (0,3) & (2,2)
\end{array}
\]

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Equilibrium (Nash)
Best responses: - If the other chooses \(N\), your best response is \(D\) (you gain market share). - If the other chooses \(D\), your best response is \(D\) (you avoid being undercut).
So \(D\) is a best response to both opponent actions: the unique Nash equilibrium is \((D,D)\).

title: Normal-form (simultaneous move)
text:
Later-on analysis

Why it matters: this is the basic logic behind price wars and “race to the bottom” outcomes.
If repeated: repeated interaction can sustain \((N,N)\) via punishments (see Repeated games).
If asymmetric costs: one café might never discount, shifting equilibrium and welfare.

title: Network games
text: In network games, each agent’s payoff depends on their action and the actions of their neighbors in a graph.

title: Network games
text: In network games, each agent’s payoff depends on their action and the actions of their neighbors in a graph.

title: Network games
text:
What’s special

Local interactions can produce global patterns (cascades, clusters).
Strategic complements/substitutes on a graph lead to amplification or dampening.
Network position (centrality) can predict influence and equilibrium actions.

title: Network games
text:
One example (linear-quadratic network game)
Let \(G\) be an adjacency matrix and actions \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A common form is:
\[
u_i(a)=\alpha a_i - \frac12 a_i^2 + \beta \sum_j G_{ij} a_i a_j.
\]
FOC for each \(i\) gives: \[
a_i = \alpha + \beta \sum_j G_{ij} a_j.
\]
In vector form: \[
a = \alpha \mathbf{1} + \beta G a
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a = (I-\beta G)^{-1}\alpha \mathbf{1},
\] when \((I-\beta G)\) is invertible.
Intuition: your action responds to neighbors; the network structure shapes equilibrium via the matrix inverse.

title: Network games
text:
Story
Study effort spreads through friendships: when your neighbors study more, you feel pressure and motivation. Your best response depends on your local network, and the network structure shapes the overall pattern.

title: Network games
text:
Model

Players are nodes in a graph with adjacency matrix \(G\)
Each chooses action \(a_i\)
Payoff has spillovers with neighbors

title: Network games
text:
Equilibrium (linear-quadratic network game)
Utility: \[
u_i(a)=\alpha a_i-\frac12 a_i^2+\beta\sum_j G_{ij}a_i a_j.
\]
FOC: \[
a_i=\alpha+\beta\sum_j G_{ij}a_j.
\]
Vector form: \[
a=\alpha\mathbf 1+\beta G a
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
a=(I-\beta G)^{-1}\alpha\mathbf 1,
\] provided \((I-\beta G)\) is invertible (a common sufficient condition is \(|\beta|<1/\rho(G)\) where \(\rho(G)\) is the spectral radius).

title: Network games
text:
Later-on analysis

Complements vs substitutes: sign of \(\beta\) changes amplification vs dampening.
Centrality: equilibrium actions often correlate with network centrality.
Interventions: targeted subsidies/penalties can propagate through the network.

title: Bayesian games
text:
A Bayesian game models incomplete information: players have private types and hold beliefs about others’ types.
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs.

title: Bayesian games
text:
A Bayesian game models incomplete information: players have private types and hold beliefs about others’ types.
A Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) is a strategy profile where each type best-responds given beliefs.

title: Bayesian games
text:
What’s special

Strategies map types to actions.
Beliefs (priors/posteriors) drive behavior.
Same strategic logic as normal-form games, but with expectations over types.

title: Bayesian games
text:
One example (2-type entry game)
Player 1 (incumbent) has type \(\theta\in\{H,L\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(H)=p\). Player 2 (entrant) chooses \(E\) (enter) or \(O\) (out). If entrant stays out: payoffs \((1,0)\).
If entrant enters: - If type is \(H\): fight is profitable for incumbent. - If type is \(L\): accommodate is better.
Toy payoff if entrant enters: - Type \(H\) incumbent prefers Fight, giving entrant payoff \(-1\). - Type \(L\) incumbent prefers Accommodate, giving entrant payoff \(+1\).
Entrant enters if expected payoff is nonnegative: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi_2 \mid E] = p(-1) + (1-p)(+1) = 1-2p \ge 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad p \le \frac12.
\]
Solution sketch. The entrant’s decision depends on the probability the incumbent is the tough type.

title: Bayesian games
text:
Story
A startup founder, Eden, pitches an angel investor. Eden knows whether the startup is strong or weak. The investor can’t fully verify this in one meeting. Funding a strong startup is profitable; funding a weak one is a loss.
The investor’s action is based on beliefs about Eden’s (hidden) type.

title: Bayesian games
text:
Model

Founder type: \(\theta\in\{S,W\}\) with prior \(\Pr(S)=p\)
Investor action: fund \(F\) or reject \(R\)
Payoff to investor: if \(F\), payoff \(+1\) under \(S\) and \(-1\) under \(W\); if \(R\), payoff \(0\)

title: Bayesian games
text:
Equilibrium (threshold best response)
Investor funds iff expected payoff is nonnegative: \[
\mathbb{E}[\pi \mid F]=p(1)+(1-p)(-1)=2p-1 \ge 0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
p\ge \tfrac12.
\]

title: Bayesian games
text:
Later-on analysis

Signals: if the pitch provides a signal, beliefs update via Bayes’ rule before the funding choice.
Strategic disclosure: if the founder can choose what to reveal, this becomes a signaling/cheap-talk hybrid.
Multiple types: richer type spaces yield cutoff strategies and comparative statics in \(p\).

title: Criminology
text:
Criminology studies crime, victimization, and social control: why harmful/illegal acts occur, how they concentrate across people and places, and how institutions (police, courts, corrections) shape incentives, behavior, and legitimacy.
This section is theory-first. Empirical findings appear mainly as stylized facts and as motivation for mechanisms and models.

title: Criminology
section: How the subject is studied (academic map)
text:
How the subject is studied (academic map)
Criminology is typically organized around three kinds of questions:

Descriptive: What patterns exist? (who/where/when crime occurs; concentration; trends)

Explanatory / causal: Why do these patterns arise? (mechanisms; incentives; social interactions; opportunity)

Evaluative / policy: What interventions change outcomes? (deterrence, prevention, rehabilitation, legitimacy)

Across these questions, research commonly moves between: - Mechanisms (theory) → clear behavioral or social channels - Evidence (empirics) → measurement, identification, evaluation - Institutions (policy context) → how rules and enforcement operate in practice

title: Opportunity & routine activity

Mechanism
The opportunity perspective treats crime as requiring: - a motivated offender, - a suitable target, - absence of capable guardianship.
Academic implication: you can reduce crime by changing the environment of opportunity (visibility, access, guardianship), even holding preferences fixed.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Mechanism (core idea)
Labeling theories emphasize that formal control can produce secondary effects: - stigma changes opportunities (labor-market access, housing), - social identity and peer grouping can shift, - repeated contact can become self-reinforcing.
In a theory-first framework, stigma is modeled as a state that affects payoffs and constraints going forward.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Canonical modeling primitives

stigma state \(z\in\{0,1\}\) (or continuous) that increases after system contact
stigma reduces legal option \(w(z)\) and/or increases network exposure to crime
feedback loop: stigma → lower \(w\) → higher crime incentives → more contact → more stigma

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
Predictions (qualitative)

Policies increasing detection/arrest can reduce crime short-run but may increase long-run crime if stigma harms future legal options.
Diversion programs and record-sealing can improve long-run outcomes by weakening the stigma transition.
The effect depends on who is marginally affected: high-risk vs low-risk populations.

title: Labeling, stigma & system contact
text:
What would count as evidence? (conceptual)
Empirical work often tries to separate: - selection into system contact vs causal impact of contact on later employment/offending, - short-run deterrence/incapacitation vs long-run stigma effects.

Mechanism
Legitimacy affects: - willingness to report victimization, - willingness to cooperate as witness, - voluntary compliance with rules.
This can be modeled as: - a participation constraint (report/cooperate only if expected benefit exceeds cost), - a utility component (disutility from cooperating with an illegitimate authority), - or a belief channel (expectations of fair treatment).

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Inspection games model strategic interaction between: - an agent who may violate (offend), and - an enforcer who can monitor/inspect at a cost.
They formalize deterrence under scarce enforcement resources.

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Canonical setup
Offender chooses \(C\) (crime) or \(N\) (no crime).
Enforcer chooses \(I\) (inspect) or \(\bar I\) (not inspect).
Parameters: - illegal gain if successful: \(b>0\) - sanction if caught: \(s>0\) - harm to enforcer if crime succeeds: \(h>0\) - inspection cost: \(k>0\)
Payoffs: - If \(N\): offender \(0\); enforcer pays \(-k\) if inspecting, \(0\) otherwise. - If \(C\) and \(I\): offender caught \(\to -s\); enforcer pays \(-k\). - If \(C\) and \(\bar I\): offender succeeds \(\to b\); enforcer suffers \(-h\).

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Solved equilibrium (mixed strategies)
Let enforcer inspect with probability \(q\) and offender commit crime with probability \(p\).

Step 1: offender indifference
\[
\mathbb{E}[u_O(C)] = q(-s) + (1-q)b = b - q(b+s).
\] Indifference with \(N\) (payoff 0) gives: \[
q^*=\frac{b}{b+s}.
\]


Step 2: enforcer indifference
Enforcer payoff from inspecting: \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(I)] = -k
\] Enforcer payoff from not inspecting: \[
\mathbb{E}[u_E(\bar I)] = -ph.
\] Indifference yields: \[
p^*=\frac{k}{h}.
\]
Interior mixing requires \(0<k<h\).

title: Inspection games (deterrence & monitoring)
text:
Predictions (comparative statics)

\(q^*\) decreases in \(s\) and increases in \(b\).
\(p^*\) increases in \(k\) and decreases in \(h\).

title: Allocation dynamics (hotspots and resource allocation)

Why dynamics matters
In practice: - the enforcer learns where problems are (updating beliefs), - offenders adapt to allocation patterns, - recorded crime reflects both incidence and reporting.
Dynamic primitives: - belief state about each location, - learning/updating, - offender adaptation, - objective function (harm vs recorded metrics).

title: Reporting & trust (legitimacy and cooperation)
text:
Canonical three-stage setup

Offender chooses \(C\) or \(N\).
If \(C\), victim chooses report \(R\) or not \(\bar R\).
If report, police choose effort \(e\in\{0,1\}\) and detection probability is: \[
q = q_0 + \alpha e,\quad q\le 1,
\] with \(q_0\in(0,1)\) and \(\alpha>0\).

Reporting cost: \(c_R>0\).
Victim benefit from detection: \(B(L)=B_0+\lambda L\) with \(\lambda>0\).
Victim reports iff: \[
(q_0+\alpha e)B(L) \ge c_R.
\]
Threshold: \[
L \ge \frac{c_R}{\lambda(q_0+\alpha e)} - \frac{B_0}{\lambda}.
\]

title: Reporting & trust (legitimacy and cooperation)
text:
Interpretation

Higher legitimacy increases reporting.
Reporting can increase recorded crime even if incidence is unchanged.
Deterrence can strengthen via higher anticipated detection.

title: Co-offending games (coordination and betrayal)
text:
Canonical stag-hunt setup
Two agents choose Join (\(J\)) or Stay out (\(O\)).

If both join: \((J,J)\) yields \(G>0\) each.
If one joins alone: joiner gets \(-d<0\), other gets \(0\).
If both stay out: \((0,0)\).

title: Co-offending games (coordination and betrayal)
text:
Equilibria
Two pure Nash equilibria: - \((J,J)\) (high-participation) - \((O,O)\) (low-participation)
Interpretation: co-offending can be self-reinforcing; small shifts in risk/coordination can change equilibrium selection.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Person-level (micro)
Typical questions: - Why do some individuals offend repeatedly? - What predicts onset/desistance?
Model primitives: - types, constraints, dynamic states (employment, stigma), discounting/self-control.
Pitfall: - selection into arrest/conviction is not identical to selection into offending.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Place-level (spatial)
Typical questions: - Why do hotspots exist? - Do interventions displace crime?
Model primitives: - opportunity/guardianship, spatial choice, congestion, displacement.
Pitfall: - shifting crime across blocks can look like “success” locally but not globally.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Network-level (social)
Typical questions: - Why co-offending clusters? - How do tactics diffuse?
Model primitives: - strategic complements, learning, partner choice, trust/betrayal, diffusion.
Pitfall: - peer effects vs sorting (who befriends whom) are easy to confuse empirically.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Institutional level (police/courts/corrections)
Typical questions: - How do agencies allocate scarce resources? - How do discretion and incentives shape outcomes?
Model primitives: - objectives, constraints, information, capacity, performance measures.
Pitfall: - “crime falls after more policing” can reflect recording/classification changes too.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Time / dynamics
Typical questions: - When does policy have short-run vs long-run effects? - How do offenders adapt?
Model primitives: - dynamic games, Markov states, learning, reputation, equilibrium adjustment.
Pitfall: - ignoring adaptation can overstate policy impact.

title: Units of analysis
text:
Practical rule
If your theory prediction is about behavior, say so.
If your prediction is about recorded outcomes, say which stage (reporting, recording, clearance, conviction) is affected.

title: Key definitions
text:
Crime, harm, and illegality

Crime: an act defined as illegal by law (jurisdiction-specific and time-varying).
Harm: a broader concept including non-criminal harms (e.g., some corporate/environmental harms).
Academic work often distinguishes: legal definitions (crime) vs normative/social definitions (harm).

Implication for theory: specify whether your model targets illegal behavior or harmful behavior more broadly.

title: Key definitions
text:
Incidence vs recorded crime

Incidence: underlying events that occur (often unobserved).
Recorded crime: events that appear in administrative data.

A stylized decomposition is:

Incidence occurs

Victim/witness chooses to report (or not)

Agency chooses to record/classify and may clear a case

Courts/corrections outcomes follow

Implication: changes in policing or trust can change recorded crime even if incidence changes less (or differently).

title: Key definitions
text:
Offending, victimization, and events

Offending: the behavior of potential offenders.
Victimization: the experience of victims (often measured via victimization surveys).
Event: a single incident; may involve multiple offenders/victims.

Implication: your unit of analysis matters (person vs event vs place).

title: Key definitions
text:
Deterrence, incapacitation, rehabilitation
Three distinct channels by which punishment/policy can reduce harm: - Deterrence: changes incentives (expected costs/benefits). - Incapacitation: reduces ability to offend (e.g., incarceration). - Rehabilitation: changes future preferences/skills/constraints (dynamic effects).
Implication: don’t conflate them—models usually represent one channel at a time.

title: Key definitions
text:
Compliance and legitimacy

Compliance: following rules/law.
Legitimacy: perceived rightfulness of authorities; affects cooperation, reporting, and voluntary compliance.

Implication: legitimacy can be modeled as shifting participation constraints (reporting/cooperation) or utility from compliance.

title: Key definitions
text:
A minimal “data caution” note
Administrative outcomes (arrests, convictions) combine: - behavior, - reporting decisions, - enforcement allocation, - legal processing rules.
When you interpret facts, always ask: “Is this about incidence, recording, or processing?”

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Criminology is not only “crime statistics.” As an academic field, it combines: - Concepts and measurement (what is counted as crime; why measurement is difficult) - Theories of mechanism (why behavior occurs; how social structure matters) - Institutional analysis (police/courts/corrections; legitimacy and compliance) - Evaluation and identification (what changes outcomes; how we infer causality)
This page provides a discipline map so readers can locate a topic within the broader research program.

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Core question types

1) Descriptive (pattern-finding)
Typical objects: - concentration by person (repeat offending/victimization), - concentration by place (hotspots), - temporal patterns (seasonality, routine changes), - network clustering (co-offending, gangs).
The descriptive layer also flags the measurement problem: recorded crime depends on reporting and enforcement.


2) Explanatory / causal (mechanism)
Mechanism-based questions: - How do incentives and detection risk affect offending? - When does opportunity/guardianship reduce crime without displacement? - How do peer effects and networks amplify or dampen crime? - How does legitimacy affect reporting and compliance?


3) Evaluative / policy (interventions)
Interventions include: - policing strategies (hotspots, visibility, patrol allocation), - sanctions and sentencing policies, - prevention programs, - rehabilitation and reentry policies, - institutional reforms targeting trust and cooperation.

title: How criminology is studied
section: Levels of analysis (what unit the theory “lives on”)
text:
Levels of analysis (what unit the theory “lives on”)
Criminological explanations often differ by unit:

Individual: preferences, beliefs, constraints, self-control, human capital

Interaction / network: strategic complements, trust, co-offending, diffusion

Place: opportunities, guardianship, environmental design, spatial displacement

Institution: rules, legitimacy, capacity, incentives within organizations

A good academic write-up states its unit explicitly and clarifies what is taken as primitive.

title: How criminology is studied
text:
Evidence types (what “counts” in the literature)
Even if you focus on theory, it helps to know what kinds of evidence usually support claims:

Administrative data: police incidents, arrests, court records, corrections

Surveys / self-reports: victimization surveys, self-reported offending

Field experiments / RCTs: randomized patrol or program assignment

Quasi-experiments: policy changes, discontinuities, natural experiments

Qualitative: interviews, ethnography, case studies (mechanism discovery)

title: How criminology is studied
section: Common threats to inference (why crime data is hard)
text:
Common threats to inference (why crime data is hard)
These issues appear repeatedly in criminology papers:

Underreporting (many crimes never enter official data)

Enforcement selection (arrests reflect policing choices)

Simultaneity (police respond to crime; crime responds to police)

Displacement (crime moves across space/time/type)

Equilibrium adaptation (offenders change tactics when policy changes)

For theory, these threats matter because they influence what is “observable” and how one interprets patterns.

title: How criminology is studied
section: How to read a criminology paper (fast checklist)
text:
How to read a criminology paper (fast checklist)
When skimming: 1) What is the unit of analysis? (person/place/network/institution)
2) What outcome is used? (incidence vs recorded vs victimization)
3) What mechanism is proposed?
4) What is the identification strategy (if empirical)?
5) What equilibrium or adaptation effects could offset the policy?
6) What predictions are robust across plausible measurement choices?
